title: India's Envoy Meets Bangladesh President as Teesta Water Diplomacy Takes Centre Stage
excerpt: High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi's first meeting with President Alamgir focused on fair sharing of common river waters ahead of the Ganga Water Treaty renewal.
body:
• Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi met Bangladesh President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir at Bangabhaban on September 8 — the first meeting between the envoy and the new president.
  • Alamgir urged India to take effective steps toward fair sharing of common river waters, including the Ganges and the Teesta, a longstanding source of bilateral tension.
  • The meeting comes weeks before the Ganga Water Treaty is due for renewal in 2026, making water diplomacy a critical issue for both nations.
  • Bangladesh's PM Tarique Rahman has been invited to attend the BRICS Summit outreach session in New Delhi on September 12–13, signalling continued diplomatic engagement.

India's High Commissioner to Bangladesh, Dinesh Trivedi, met President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir at Bangabhaban on Tuesday in what was the first meeting between the Indian envoy and the newly inaugurated president. The meeting comes as both countries navigate a delicate diplomatic reset, with shared river management, trade and the upcoming BRICS Summit driving the agenda.

Water Diplomacy Takes Centre Stage

The most substantive issue raised during the meeting was the management of shared rivers. President Alamgir urged India to take "effective steps toward the fair sharing of common river waters, including the Ganges and Teesta," according to a Bangabhaban statement carried by ANI. Trivedi told the president that "positive measures were being taken" by the Indian government on the matter.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=2bRG6DG_dDY

"Reaching fair and mutually acceptable solutions to matters of shared interest would further enhance trust and confidence among the people of both nations."

— Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir, President of Bangladesh

The Teesta water-sharing agreement has remained a sticking point in India-Bangladesh relations for decades. The river flows from Sikkim through West Bengal into Bangladesh, and negotiations over an equitable sharing formula have repeatedly stalled. The Ganga Water Treaty, signed in 1996, is due for renewal in 2026, adding urgency to the water diplomacy track.

A significant development this year has been India's appointment of Trivedi, a veteran politician with deep roots in West Bengal politics, as its envoy to Dhaka. Analysts have read this as New Delhi signalling intent for direct engagement on sensitive bilateral issues, particularly water sharing, which hinges heavily on West Bengal's cooperation. The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party's first-ever election victory in West Bengal in May 2026 has also shifted the political dynamic, creating what some call a "double-engine government" that could ease the path for river agreements, according to Eco-Business.

Resetting Ties After Political Upheaval

The diplomatic engagement comes against the backdrop of Bangladesh's transition to a new government led by the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP). Alamgir took the oath as the 23rd president on August 21, and the meeting with Trivedi was part of a broader sequence of Indian diplomatic outreach.

Trivedi had previously met Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on August 10, where both sides discussed issues of mutual interest. Following that meeting, the Indian High Commission posted on X that the discussions focused on "avenues for further strengthening bilateral relations between India and Bangladesh with a people-centric approach." Rahman has been invited to attend the BRICS Summit outreach session in New Delhi this week, according to Indian media reports.

Relations between the two countries had been strained by India's harbouring of deposed former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, and the new BNP government has emphasised a "Bangladesh First" policy built on "sovereign equality, mutual trust and mutual benefit." India responded with key gestures including the restoration of visa services and Trivedi's high-profile appointment.

Broader Bilateral Agenda

Beyond rivers, President Alamgir told Trivedi there was "significant scope to deepen bilateral cooperation in trade, water management, technology, connectivity, culture and people-to-people ties," according to the President's Press Secretary Md Sarwar Alam, as reported by Bangladeshi outlet UNB.

Bangladesh currently has more than 40 bilateral mechanisms with India covering trade, border management, consular issues and water-sharing. India is willing to engage the new government by "gradually reactivating all the bilateral mechanisms," according to diplomatic sources cited by UNB.

Last month, Indian President Droupadi Murmu sent a congratulatory message to Alamgir, noting that "bilateral ties have steadily expanded to several areas such as energy, technology, connectivity, youth affairs, health and education." The Indian High Commission in Dhaka described the Tuesday meeting as underscoring "the deep-rooted bonds between India and Bangladesh, built on shared history, close cultural ties and people-to-people relations."

What's Next

The trajectory of India-Bangladesh relations over the coming months will depend on concrete progress on river water sharing. The Ganga Water Treaty renewal is the most time-sensitive item, while any breakthrough on the Teesta — even a framework agreement — could transform public opinion in Bangladesh, where the issue is deeply felt. With the BRICS Summit outreach session offering another opportunity for high-level engagement between Modi and Rahman, September could prove pivotal in defining the terms of the new bilateral relationship.
